title: Python Foundations
description: Check that the base the rest of the course builds on is solid.

lessons.title: Types, control flow, and strings
lessons.lead: Four questions on the grammar of Python  the parts every later module assumes you already know.

questions.explain: `int()` truncates toward zero  it drops the decimal part rather than rounding. Use `round(87.5)` when you want rounding.

questions.prompt: How many lines does this loop print?
questions.explain: `range(1, 4)` yields 1, 2, 3  the stop value is never included. This off-by-one catches everyone once.

questions.prompt: What defines a block of code in Python?
options: A semicolon at the end of each line
questions.explain: Indentation is the syntax, not a style choice. Four spaces per level is the convention.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about Python strings are true?
options: `.split(",")` turns one line into a list of fields
An f-string can format a value inline, as in `f"{score:.1f}"`
questions.explain: Strings are immutable  `.lower()` returns a new string and leaves the original untouched. You have to assign the result.

lessons.title: Parameters, defaults, and scope
lessons.lead: Functions are how logic gets named and reused. These questions cover the traps that come with them.

questions.prompt: Given this function, what does `grade(41, passing=40)` return?
questions.explain: 41 >= 40, so status is "pass", and `label` keeps its default of "student".

questions.prompt: What does a function return when it has no `return` statement?
questions.explain: Every Python function returns something. With no `return`, that something is `None`.

questions.prompt: Why should you never write `def add_item(item, items=[])`?
options: The same list is created once and shared across every call
Lists are not allowed as default arguments
It is significantly slower than passing the list in
questions.explain: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined. Use `items=None` and create the list inside the body.

questions.prompt: Calling `grade(72)` and then `print(status)` outside the function raises NameError. Why?
options: `status` only exists inside the function that created it
The function has to be called twice first
questions.explain: Variables created inside a function are local to it. If you need the value outside, return it.

lessons.title: Order versus lookup
lessons.lead: The two containers you will use every day, and the moment to reach for each one.

questions.explain: Slices start at the first index and stop before the second  positions 1 and 2, not 3.
`.get()` returns the default you supply when the key is missing, instead of raising KeyError the way `student["email"]` would.

options: A list keeps its items in the order they were added
Reading a missing key with `d["key"]` raises KeyError
Assigning to a key that does not exist adds it to the dictionary
A list can only be indexed from the front
questions.explain: `scores[-1]` reads the last item  negative indexes count back from the end.

questions.prompt: Which shape is the usual way to represent a table of records in plain Python?
options: A list of lists of strings
A single dictionary with numeric keys
questions.explain: One dictionary is one row; a list of them is the table. This is exactly what a Pandas DataFrame wraps in Module 04.

lessons.title: Getting data in and out
lessons.lead: Reading files safely, and the one thing everybody forgets about CSV values.

questions.prompt: Why open files with `with open(...) as f:` rather than a plain `open()`?
options: The file is closed automatically, even if the code raises an error
It is the only way to pass an encoding
It converts the file to a list of strings
questions.explain: The `with` block closes the file on the way out, whether the body finished normally or raised.

questions.prompt: What does mode `"w"` do to a file that already exists?
options: Overwrites it  the previous contents are gone
Appends to the end of it
questions.explain: `"w"` truncates the file. Use `"a"` when you mean to add to what is already there.

questions.prompt: What type are the values that come out of `csv.DictReader`?
options: Guessed per column  numbers become `int` or `float`
questions.explain: Every CSV value arrives as a string. Converting types on the way in  `float(row["score"])`  prevents a whole category of bugs later.

questions.prompt: Which are good practice when reading a text file?
options: Pass `encoding="utf-8"` so Khmer and other non-ASCII text survives
Strip the trailing newline from each line before using it
Loop over the file object directly for a large file
Use `.read()` to pull a 2 GB file into one string
questions.explain: `.read()` loads the whole file into memory at once. Looping over the file object reads it line by line instead.
